title: Scoliosis Support and Exercise in Sarasota, FL | MD Fit
h1: Scoliosis Support and Posture Care in Sarasota, FL
description: Living with scoliosis in Sarasota. Exercise and soft-tissue care alongside your specialist, to keep you strong, mobile and comfortable with the curve.
lead: Scoliosis is a sideways curve and rotation of the spine, diagnosed and monitored by a physician. What MD Fit offers runs alongside that specialist care: keeping you strong, mobile and comfortable living with the curve you have.

sections.h2: What this page does and does not claim
sections.html:
To be clear about scope, because this is an area where people are promised a great deal: no exercise programme here straightens a structural curve. Curve magnitude is measured on imaging and managed by a specialist, and in growing adolescents bracing and surgical decisions belong firmly with them.

What movement-based care does reliably offer is strength, mobility, breathing capacity and pain management. For many adults living with a curve, those are the things that determine how the day actually goes.

A curved spine loads muscles asymmetrically. One side works lengthened and the other shortened, all day, for years. The result is predictable patterns of fatigue and ache:

  • Quadratus lumborum on the concave side, shortened and tender, referring into the flank and upper buttock.
  • Iliocostalis and longissimus working unevenly along the length of the back.
  • Multifidus, the deep segmental stabiliser, often poorly recruited where the rotation is greatest.
  • Shoulder and rib asymmetry, producing pain between the shoulder blades and sometimes rib discomfort with deep breathing.

Importantly, pain level and curve size correlate poorly. Plenty of people with significant curves are comfortable, and plenty with mild ones are not.

Dr. Jared assesses how you move rather than measuring your curve, which your specialist has already done. He looks at hip and thoracic mobility, breathing mechanics, where the muscles are overworking, and how you load each side in standing and walking.

Hands-on work releases the muscles taking the asymmetric load, which often eases the daily ache considerably. Mobility work targets the stiff segments, including the ribs, since rib stiffness limits breathing on the concave side. Breathing work is a genuine part of this rather than an afterthought.

Then strength, which is the part that matters most for an adult spine. Loading is progressed carefully and symmetrically where possible, and daily routines come through the free MD Fit app.

People with scoliosis are often advised, informally, to avoid loading their spine. That advice tends to produce a weaker spine, which copes worse rather than better.

Smart, coached loading is one of the better things available for an adult spine with a curve: it maintains bone density, builds the muscular support the spine relies on, and preserves function into later decades. The coaching part matters, because technique and progression have to account for how your spine actually moves.

sections.h2: Who should be seen elsewhere first
sections.html:
Dr. Jared sees adults and older teens. A child or younger adolescent with a newly noticed curve should be assessed by a paediatric scoliosis specialist first, because growth changes everything about the decision-making and the window for bracing is time-sensitive.

Anyone with a curve that appears to be progressing, new neurological symptoms, or significant breathing difficulty needs specialist review rather than exercise care. Post-surgical spines are worked with according to the surgeon's protocol and restrictions.

1. Move often and vary your positions. Static holding is what aggravates an asymmetric spine.
  2. Breathe deliberately into the side that feels restricted, a few minutes a day.
  3. Keep strength training, with coaching.
  4. Carry bags across the body or in a backpack rather than always on one side.

The goal is a spine that works, not a spine that looks different on an X-ray.

redFlags: New or rapidly progressing curve, especially in a child or adolescent, which needs specialist review promptly.
New numbness, weakness, or changes in bladder or bowel function: this needs urgent medical assessment.
Shortness of breath that is new or worsening, which needs medical review.
Severe back pain that is constant, unrelated to position, and wakes you at night.
Back pain with fever or unexplained weight loss.

faq.a: No single exercise straightens a structural curve. The goal is to keep you strong, mobile and breathing well so you can live comfortably with the curve.
Yes, with coaching. Smart loading is one of the better things available for an aging spine with a curve.

faq.q: Do you treat kids and teens?
faq.a: Dr. Jared sees adults and older teens. Younger children are referred to a paediatric scoliosis specialist first.

faq.q: Does a bigger curve mean more pain?
faq.a: Not reliably. Pain and curve size correlate poorly, which is why treatment is built around your symptoms and function rather than the number on your imaging report.
